title: Measured silent defects in widely used npm packages
note: Every entry was reproduced locally against the version named in `measuredAgainst`, which was the latest published version at the time of the audit. `reproduce` is runnable as written. Where a prior report exists in the project's own tracker it is linked, and where a documented setting changes the behaviour the entry says so. Nothing here is inferred from documentation or issue trackers; the trackers were searched only to give credit where a report already exists.

findings.headline: bytes.parse('5MiB') returns 5
findings.detail: The README lists the supported units as b, kb, mb, gb, tb and pb, and documents parse as returning a number or null. An IEC unit such as MiB is not among them — support has been an open request since 2015 — but an IEC string is not refused with null as the contract implies. It is parsed as its leading number, so an express body limit written limit: '5MiB' becomes a five-byte limit and every request is rejected. bytes is what body-parser uses.
findings.affectsYouIf: you pass a size string containing KiB, MiB, GiB or TiB to anything backed by bytes — express/body-parser limits, multer, or your own config
findings.workaround: Use a plain byte count, or a parser that understands IEC units.

priorReports.note: asks for IEC units to be supported; does not mention that an IEC string is currently parsed as its leading number

findings.headline: bytes and bytes-iec return different numbers for the same string
findings.detail: bytes reads 1MB as 1,048,576, the binary convention; bytes-iec reads it as 1,000,000, the SI standard. They are 2.4% apart at kB, 4.9% at MB, 7.4% at GB and 10% at TB, always in the direction of allowing more than was written. Neither README states which convention it uses, so swapping one for the other silently resizes every limit already deployed.
findings.affectsYouIf: you have both in a dependency tree, or you are migrating between them
findings.workaround: Write IEC units (MiB) when you mean binary sizes; they are unambiguous in bytes-iec, though see the finding above for bytes.

findings.headline: bytes answers unreadable input with a number
findings.detail: Measured over 17 unreadable strings, bytes returned a number for 13 of them rather than the documented null.
findings.reproduce:
const b = require('bytes');
b.parse('1,5MB')     // 1
b.parse('10 MB 5')   // 10
b.parse('0x10MB')    // 0
b.parse('1XB')       // 1
findings.affectsYouIf: a size can come from a human-edited config file or an environment variable
findings.workaround: Validate the string before parsing it.

findings.headline: flat destroys a value when a key contains the delimiter
findings.detail: Flattening and unflattening is only useful if it round-trips. A key containing a dot collides with the path separator and one of the two values is lost. Keys with dots are ordinary: i18n message ids, hostnames, metric names, CSV headers. Escaping has been an open request since 2018; the transformKey option suggested there as the answer does not work for this, because unflatten splits on the delimiter before applying it — measured: {'a.b': 1, a: {b: 2}} escaped with transformKey comes back as {'a\\': {b: 1}, a: {b: 2}}.
findings.reproduce:
const {flatten, unflatten} = require('flat');
unflatten(flatten({'a.b': 1, a: {b: 2}}))  // {a: {b: 2}} — the first value is gone
findings.affectsYouIf: you flatten objects whose keys can contain a dot, a bracket or a backslash
findings.workaround: Use a flattener that escapes keys; there is no setting in flat that makes this round-trip.

priorReports.note: asks for delimiter escaping; a later comment suggests transformKey, which does not round-trip

findings.headline: flat turns an object with numeric keys into a sparse array
findings.detail: There is no option that keeps both: the default turns numeric-keyed objects into arrays, and {object: true} turns every array into an object. Across 25 fixtures the default kept 13 and {object: true} kept 11. This exact behaviour has been reported and open since 2020.
findings.affectsYouIf: your objects can be keyed by ids, indices or anything numeric
findings.workaround: None within flat; the trade is structural.

priorReports.note: the same behaviour, reported with the same example

findings.headline: deserializeError is exponential in the depth of the cause chain
findings.detail: 0.4 ms at depth 5, 10.6 ms at 10, 339 ms at 15 and 11 seconds at depth 20, on a payload of 6.6 KB. In destroyCircular, `cause` is walked once in the Object.keys loop and again in the errorProperties loop, and seen.delete(from) makes cycle detection path-based rather than memoised, so the two paths compound to 2^depth. Serializing is fast because `cause` is non-enumerable on a real Error; a JSON round trip makes it enumerable, which is exactly the worker-to-main-thread path the library exists for. A different performance problem in the same function — copying the `seen` array on every recursion — was reported and fixed in 13.0.1; this one is present in that release.
findings.affectsYouIf: you wrap errors with `cause` through several layers and send them across a boundary as JSON
findings.workaround: Cap the cause chain before serialising, or use a serialiser that handles errors iteratively.

priorReports.note: a different bottleneck in destroyCircular (O(n²) copying of the seen array), fixed in 13.0.1; the exponential cause walk is separate and remains

findings.headline: parse-duration reads '1,5h' as fifteen hours under its default locale
findings.detail: Under the default English locale a comma is a thousands separator, so one and a half hours written the way most of the world writes it becomes fifteen hours — a ten-fold error, silently. This one is configurable: the decimal separator can be changed with parse.unit = {...en, decimal: ','}, and the bundled de, es, fr and pt locales already do so. The README documents only switching to a whole locale, not setting the separator, so the default is what most callers get.
findings.affectsYouIf: durations come from human-edited config and your users are not all using a dot as the decimal point
findings.workaround: Set the decimal separator: parse.unit = {...en, decimal: ','}. Note that mutating parse.unit.decimal in place does not take effect; assign a new object.

priorReports.note: asked for a configurable decimal separator; the unit object now carries one, though the README does not mention it

findings.headline: parse-duration drops the day from a valid ISO 8601 duration, and reads P1M as one minute
findings.detail: P1DT2H returns two hours; the day is gone. And P1M (one month) and PT1M (one minute) both return 60000, because M means months before the T and minutes after it. A monthly retention window becomes a one-minute one. No setting changes this.
findings.affectsYouIf: you accept ISO 8601 durations from an API, a JSON Schema, or a calendar feed
findings.workaround: Parse ISO durations with a dedicated ISO parser.

findings.headline: croner fires an hourly job twice at the same instant across spring forward
findings.detail: '0 * * * *' in America/New_York on 2026-03-08 yields 24 fires for a 23-hour day, emitting 2026-03-08T07:00:00Z twice. cron-parser gives 23 for the same expression. Several DST problems have been reported and fixed in croner; this one reproduces on the latest stable release and on the 10.0.2-dev.3 and 11.0.0-dev.0 prereleases that carry those fixes.
findings.affectsYouIf: you run sub-daily jobs in a timezone that observes daylight saving, and running twice is not safe
findings.workaround: Make the job idempotent, or use cron-parser to compute occurrences.

priorReports.note: a different DST problem (second-interval skipping), fixed in 10.0.2-dev.0; the duplicate hourly fire is not covered by that fix

findings.headline: superjson silently loses sparse arrays, ArrayBuffers, null-prototype objects, and an error's class
findings.detail: Over 27 fixtures, superjson returned a changed value without error for sparse arrays (holes become undefined), ArrayBuffer (becomes a plain object), and null-prototype objects (gain a prototype). The README lists Error as supported, and the message does survive, but the class does not: a TypeError comes back as a plain Error even with allowErrorProps. Class instances are not counted here — the README says built-ins only by default, and registerClass restores them, which was measured to work. devalue, measured on the same fixtures, had zero silent losses: it is either exact or it throws.
findings.affectsYouIf: you send error subclasses, binary data, sparse arrays or null-prototype objects across a superjson boundary — a tRPC call, for instance
findings.workaround: Register a custom transformer for those types, or use devalue.

findings.headline: timestring returns a positive number for a negative duration
findings.detail: '-5m' returns +300000. Negative durations were proposed in 2014 and never implemented, so they are unsupported — but the sign is silently dropped rather than the input being refused. enhanced-ms behaves the same way.
findings.affectsYouIf: durations in your system can be negative — an offset, a drift correction, a relative time
findings.workaround: Handle the sign yourself before parsing.

priorReports.note: proposed negative support; closed for inactivity without implementing it

findings.headline: rrule returns the wrong instant when the machine's own timezone changes on the same day as the target zone
findings.detail: A daily 09:00 recurrence in America/New_York is correct every day except the spring-forward day, where it points an hour early — 08:00 instead of 09:00. rrule's documented model routes a TZID result through the system timezone, and the error appears only when the system zone also transitions that day. Measured correct under TZ=UTC, Asia/Tokyo and Europe/London, and wrong under America/Los_Angeles. On a UTC container it is right, so it passes in CI and fires early in production once a year. No prior report of this was found.
findings.affectsYouIf: you schedule recurrences with a TZID and your process runs in a timezone that observes daylight saving
findings.workaround: Run the process in UTC, or use rrule-temporal, which was measured correct on all of these.
